Fraudulent or suspicious payout requests may be processed without FCU referral where fraud indicators are present (non-source bank accounts, identity mismatches, duplicate requests, suspicious documents), resulting in financial loss, regulatory non-compliance, and reputational damage.

Assessment (Quality Check) stage includes process for identifying fraud triggers and their assessment. Any fraudulent or suspicious case identified during document scrutiny immediately referred to FCU team for investigation before payout processing. FCU report awaited; case not processed until positive FCU clearance obtained (deviation matrix: positive FCU report required as one of three acceptable deviations). Video verification (outsourced) used as additional verification layer for Red RAG cases (≥₹2L). Non-contactable customers also referred to FCU. Checker verifies fraud trigger assessment before approving in BPOS. All FCU referrals documented and tracked to closure.
Delayed / Inaccurate Regulatory Reporting to IRDAI

Failure to submit accurate and timely regulatory returns to IRDAI (claims ageing, unclaimed ageing, settlement progress, L-39, L-40, penal interest, statewise benefits paid, Form A & B) may result in regulatory penalties, IRDAI scrutiny, and governance failures. Inaccurate MIS may mask process gaps.

Business MIS/PPT/PPC reviewed monthly by Management. Regulatory reports submitted to IRDAI quarterly: Claims Ageing Data, Claims Movement Data, Statewise Benefits Paid Movement, Ageing of Unclaimed Amounts, Progress of Settlement of Unclaimed Amount, L-39, L-40, Penal Interest Paid (Claims & Benefits), Ageing of Survival/Maturity Benefits. Finance Reconciliation MIS reviewed monthly. Unclaimed Report reviewed daily. Life Asia Payout Pending Report reviewed daily. Form A & B with Policyholders' Protection Committee minutes submitted to IRDAI half-yearly. Concurrent Auditor verifies unclaimed amounts quarterly. All MIS and reports retained for audit purposes.
Adherence of Fraud Prevention Policy with IRDA fraud prevention rules and regulations
Absence or Non-Review of Board-Approved Anti-Fraud Policy

If the company does not maintain a Board-approved Anti-Fraud Policy aligned with IRDAI Circular IRDA/SDD/MISC/CIR/009/01/2013, or fails to review it periodically, the fraud risk management framework will lack regulatory grounding. This results in regulatory non-compliance, inadequate fraud controls, and exposure to reputational and financial loss across the product lifecycle (new business, servicing, payouts, claims).

1. The Company has formulated an Anti-Fraud Policy in accordance with IRDAI guidelines, duly approved by the Board of Directors. The policy emphasises prevention and detection of frauds through early warning symptoms and prompt corrective measures.
2. The SOP (SUDL-FCU-PR-01 v1.9) complements the policy (v1.9) and details responsibilities of each FCU role across the fraud lifecycle (incident reporting to closure). 
3. FCU prepares the Internal Financial Control Sheet (IFCS) annually in coordination with Internal Audit. 
4. Fraud controls are reviewed yearly using a RAG scoring matrix (Red/Amber/Green).
Inadequate Fraud Awareness Leading to Undetected / Unreported Frauds

If employees are not mandated to participate in fraud awareness training or are unaware of the Fraud Responsibility Matrix and reporting channels, frauds may go undetected or unreported within their areas of responsibility/control, increasing financial loss and regulatory non-compliance.

1. Every employee is mandated to participate in the fraud awareness training programme. 
2. Broad scope: basic awareness, sales conduct, adherence to agents' code of conduct. FCU imparts training through: publishing modules on intranet; Train the Trainer programme for sales trainers for onward field training. 
3. Annual Training Calendar prepared (Annexure F). Fraud Responsibility Matrix (Annexure E) defines each employee's reporting obligation. 
4. Material fraud or suspected fraud to be reported to FCU immediately upon detection. 
5. FCU MIS (monthly/quarterly) and RMC/Board Report (quarterly) shared with business heads and regional teams with observations and recommendations.
Review of Fraud Identification and reporting process across high-risk functions
Fraudulent New Business Policies Issued Due to Inadequate Pre-Issuance Verification

New business proposals with document tampering, medical non-disclosure, misrepresentation, Aadhaar authentication fraud, income/occupation mismatch, or impersonation may be issued without adequate investigation by underwriting, resulting in adverse selection, fraudulent policies in-force, and significant future claim losses.

1. Underwriting department refers pre-issuance cases to FCU through Omni Flow and email.
2. FCU assigns cases to empanelled external investigation agencies (selected per expertise, geographic reach, efficiency, accuracy, and quality; TAT defined in SLA). 
3. Agency investigates: complete profile of life assured (age, qualification, occupation, family, income, health); KYC, income proof, and medical document verification. 
4. Investigation report categorised as Positive/Negative. Negative triggers: age discrepancy, income/occupation mismatch, lifestyle risk, medical non-disclosure, BMI deviation, document forgery, death prior to proposal, impersonation/identity theft/multiple identities, customer non-existence, misselling. 
5. Findings shared with Underwriting via Omni Flow/email;
6. UW initiates policy-level action. Where FCU finding differs from UW decision, clarity is sought. 
7. Negative investigation employee cases escalated to DPC per Anti-Fraud Policy Disciplinary Action Matrix. 
8. FCU maintains daily tracker; consolidated MIS shared with Head-FCU regularly.
9. Aadhaar fraud findings reported immediately to CISO and Head – Compliance & Legal.
Review of Fraud Identification and reporting process across high-risk functions
Identity Fraud, Account Takeover, and Organised Application Fraud Not Detected at Issuance Stage

Without proactive FCU eyeballing of new business issuances, cases of identity fraud, account takeover, and organised application fraud by syndicates may go undetected, resulting in fraudulent policies being in-force, future fraudulent claim payouts, and regulatory non-compliance.

1. Issuance data downloaded from BI Portal. 
2. Dynamic parameters applied for case selection (reviewed and modified per emerging fraud trends): exclude zero-risk policies; include policies with Premium/Sum Assured/SUC ratio >10; exclude premiums ≥₹2L; exclude SUC ≤₹3L; include all non-Banca channel issuances. 
3. Expert FCU sampler eyeballs selected applications using Eyeballing/Sampling Checklist (Annexure H). 
4. Eyeballing remarks updated in MIS. 
5. Doubtful cases triggered for external agency investigation (basis expertise and geographic reach). 
6. Investigation report classified as Positive/Negative/Refer to Underwriter. 
7. Underwriting reviews negative cases and initiates CFI, further requirements/alter from inception, or risk acceptance. FCU consolidated tracker maintained; regularly shared with Head-FCU. 
8. High-risk negative cases (e.g., prior death): clarification from employee; unsatisfactory explanation referred to HR and DPC process followed.
Review of Fraud Identification and reporting process across high-risk functions
Fraudulent Individual Retail Death Claims Paid Without Detection

Fraudulent individual death claims (based on pre-DOC death, medical non-disclosure, document forgery, impersonation, fabricated death certificates) may be paid without detection if analytical fraud models are not deployed at the pre-disbursal stage, resulting in financial loss, fraudulent claim settlement, and regulatory scrutiny.

1. Individual claims data extracted from BI Portal daily (T day). 
2. BIU runs three statistical fraud detection models (T+1, morning): Medical-STP Fail; Non-Medical I-STP Pass; Non-Medical II-STP Fail. Models use categorical (gender, cause/type of death, age) and numerical attributes (premium, sum assured, annual income) plus demographic characteristics. 
3. Early claim cases run into Excel-based models (Macro enabled). 
4. Model-selected cases reviewed individually with claim documents.
5. Cases allocated to external agencies for field investigation. On receipt of full investigation report, FCU reviews and shares findings/decision with claims team (T+15 to T+60). 
6. Investigation classified Positive/Negative. Negative triggers: age discrepancy, medical non-disclosure, BMI deviation, document forgery, death prior to proposal, impersonation/identity theft/multiple identities. 
7. Repudiated/CFI cases: clarification from salesperson; unsatisfactory explanation reported to HR and DPC. 
8. FCU also picks cases through manual eyeballing outside model.
9. Positive cases randomly reinvestigated monthly for quality assurance. 
10. Claims team may refer any suspicious claim to FCU independently.
Review of Fraud Identification and reporting process across high-risk functions
Fraudulent PMJJBY Group Death Claims Paid Without Pre-Disbursal Screening

PMJJBY claims (government scheme) are particularly susceptible to organised fraud (fake death certificates, dual death certificates, death prior to member enrolment, impersonation). Without pre-disbursal eyeballing and field investigation, fraudulent claims may be settled resulting in financial loss and regulatory non-compliance with PMJJBY scheme guidelines.

1. PMJJBY death claims data downloaded from BI Portal (T day). 2. BIU runs analytical PMJJBY fraud detection model (T+1, morning). Model output evaluated; cases selected for eyeballing. Algorithm basis: all early death claims where insured death occurred ≤365 days from member enrolment date considered for eyeballing. 
3. Red cases (model-flagged): claims team intimated, FCU investigation required, claim held. 
4. Expert FCU sampler eyeballs Amber/Green cases manually. 5. Suspicious Amber/Green cases: claims team intimated, claim held. 
6. Non-suspicious cases: claims process continues per SOP. 
7. Doubtful cases assigned to external agencies. Investigation classified Positive/Negative. Negative triggers: age discrepancy, fake/dual death certificate, death prior to member enrolment, impersonation/identity theft/multiple identities. 
8. FCU findings and decision shared with claims team (T+5 for PMJJBY). 
9. Daily MIS shared with claims team. 
10. Entire PMJJBY eyeballing/sampling currently in manual mode; model being improved for reimplementation post validation.
Fraudulent Grievances (Premium Misappropriation, Forgery, Hoax Calls) Not Investigated Timely or Action Not Initiated

Grievances involving premium misappropriation (cheque/DD used in another policy), document/signature forgery, and hoax calls (vishing, impersonation of IRDAI/insurer) that are not referred to FCU, investigated inadequately, or where employee/agent involvement is not actioned through DPC, result in customer financial loss, regulatory non-compliance, and reputational damage.

1. Cases involving premium misappropriation, document forgery/tampering, signature forgery, and hoax calls reported to FCU by grievance team (via fraudcontrolunit@sudlife.in). 
2. FCU investigates; seeks clarification from concerned branch/person or independent feedback from reporting supervisor if person not available in system. 
3. FCU findings with necessary evidence provided to grievance department in prescribed format. 
4. Cases where employee/agent involvement is proven: details reported to Disciplinary Committee (DPC) for action per malpractice matrix. 
5. HR issues action letter/show-cause notice per disciplinary process.
Sales Non-Compliances (Mis-selling, Incorrect Customer Data, Signature Mismatch) Not Detected / Actioned

Sales non-compliances such as incorrect customer contact information captured by sales officers, need-based suitability analysis not conducted, signature mismatch on policy documents, and repeated discrepant data patterns (multiple customer records with identical contact/bank account details) may go undetected without systematic exception monitoring, leading to mis-selling complaints, fraudulent claims, business leakages, and regulatory penalties.

1. FCU uses analytics and control reports (rules in SQL, SAS, data warehouse) to generate exception reports from application and transaction data (Life Asia, Omni-flow, UBP, Claims register, FCU MIS) monthly. 
2. Exception rules and triggers reviewed periodically; new rules added/discontinued as per experience. 
3. Policy-wise discrepancies identified (e.g., multiple customer records with identical contact/bank account details). 
4. Discrepant cases taken up for clarification from sourcing sales officer, looping in reporting manager/branch operations executive. 
5. Generic email salescompliance@sudlife.in monitored daily by sales compliance team. Responses received, reviewed, and closed in FRMS. 
6. Reminder emails sent where response not received. 
7. Confirmed malpractice cases reported to HR and DPC process followed. 
8. Root cause analysis conducted; corrective actions initiated (employee training, customer awareness, process improvement, disciplinary action)
Frauds and Suspicious Activities Not Reported Through Dedicated Channels / Not Actioned Within TAT

If frauds or suspicious activities detected by any department (Claims, Grievance, Distribution, Regions, Zones, Branches) are not reported to FCU through the dedicated email channels, or if FCU does not record and action them within TAT, fraud incidents remain unaddressed, leading to financial loss, regulatory non-compliance, and loss of deterrent effect.

1. Dedicated email IDs maintained: fraudcontrolunit@sudlife.in (reporting frauds immediately on detection); salescompliance@sudlife.in (reporting suspicious activities/sales non-compliances). 
2. Both monitored daily. 
3. On receipt, case details recorded in daily tracker/FRMS for follow-up and closure within TAT. 
4. FCU conducts preliminary investigation to gather first-hand facts and, if required, assigns to respective investigating agencies per defined criteria. 
5. On receipt of investigation report, FCU responds to respective channel with findings and recommendations. 
6. Every instance of material fraud (loss >₹7L) reported to management within 7 days from detection with interim findings. RMC/Board Report submitted quarterly.
Loss Accounting & Recovery: Recognition of fraud losses, recovery tracking, write-off governance
Employee/Agent Premium Misappropriation Not Investigated, Recovered, or Written Off Per Policy

Premium misappropriation by employees or agents (fund misused from customer policies) that is not investigated promptly, not actioned through HR/DPC, not reported to law enforcement for amounts above ₹50,000, or not properly accounted for (provision/write-off) results in unrecovered financial losses, incorrect books of accounts, and regulatory non-compliance.

1. FCU investigates reported premium misappropriation cases. 2. Actions: employee action through HR/DPC; recovery from employee/agent; fidelity insurance claim with General Insurance Company; legal action (demand notice → legal notice → police complaint/FIR for cases ≥₹50,000 per approved office note 
3. Fidelity claim documents: claim form; office mail/note for infusion; customer complaint and pay-in slips; demand/legal notice; FIR copy; employee appointment letter and last 3 salary slips. 
4. Fidelity settlement amount informed to Finance for accounting entries. 
5. FCU tracks all losses for recovery periodically; regular follow-up with law enforcement for deterrent action. 
6. Write-off criteria: (i) 3 years elapsed from fraud date/FIR; same modus operandi and amount ≤₹1L; (ii) substantial portion recovered via fidelity; (iii) amount ≤₹50,000 with terminated/exited employee post demand+legal notice. 
7. All write-offs per financial DOA. Provision made in books for all cases.
Remittance Fraud Not Detected Due to Absence of Independent Surveillance on Payouts

Without independent FCU surveillance on policy remittance payouts, fraud abnormalities (contact number/bank account changes near payout, mismatches between payout and issuance documents, IMPS process bypassed for ineligible bank types) may go undetected, reinforcing existing control gaps in the payout process.

1. FCU selects sample from processed payouts based on risk parameters: type of payout, payout amount, bank account provided for payout, source bank account. 
2. Month-on-month: samples picked from data and verified in Sales Force for recent changes in contact number and account details. 
3. Documents submitted for payout cross-validated (eyeballing) with documents submitted at issuance (photograph, signature, KYC, account details). 
4. Flat files checked to tally account details with initial/source account from issuance/renewal vs. payout account. IMPS process validated: sample cross-referencing of payout data with IMPS data; IMPS failures for Gramin/Cooperative banks (not IMPS-enabled) identified. 
5. Any discrepancy: case thoroughly checked and cross-verified with all payout parameters. 
6. Monthly report prepared on samples verified and outcomes. FCU checks adherence of preventive checklist by remittance processing unit; findings and recommendations shared with process owners regularly.
Review Implementation of Corrective Actions & Disciplinary Action taken as per Disciplinary Action Matrix
Fictitious or Inflated Employee Expense Reimbursements Processed Without Detection

Employee expense fraud (falsified/manipulated receipts, inflated bills, billing for non-materialised travel, seeking reimbursement for unpurchased items, collusion to process unauthorised reimbursements) may be processed without detection, resulting in financial loss and deterioration of internal controls.

1. FCU obtains list of employee reimbursement claims for the quarter from Accounts (via EMS). 
2. Physical documents (bills/invoices/receipts) with payout details selected for eyeballing per pre-defined parameters. 3. Selection criteria (dynamic triggers): spelling mistakes, overwriting, same bill number used for multiple bills, tax calculation errors; plus amount variance, type of claim, role of person, geographical location. 
4. High conveyance bills evaluated per geographical distance and average service provider charges. 
5. Up to 10% of selected samples sent for field verification through specialised investigation agencies. 
6. Fraudulent claims/document forgery: explanation sought from employee; unsatisfactory or absent explanation → DPC issues warning/action per HR policy; findings reported to HR. 
7. Physical documents returned to Accounts after eyeballing. 
8. MIS and dashboards maintained. Activity performed annually (minimum) depending on data availability; report published thereafter.
Review Implementation of Corrective Actions & Disciplinary Action taken as per Disciplinary Action Matrix
Misuse of Aadhaar Framework or Compromise of Aadhaar Systems Not Detected or Reported Timely

Every instance of attempted or actual misuse of Aadhaar information/systems (including Aadhaar-based authentication for new retail life insurance policies in the name of deceased or absent customers) that is not immediately reported to CISO, Head-Compliance & Legal, UIDAI, and the Aadhaar holder poses a risk of regulatory breach under the Aadhaar Act, data privacy violations, and fraud facilitation.

1. Every instance of attempted/actual misuse of Aadhaar information or systems reported by FCU to CISO and Head – Compliance, Legal & FCU immediately upon detection (no delay). 
2. If FCU identifies a fraud pattern related to Aadhaar authentication through fraud analytics/investigations/triggers: all necessary details reported to CISO and Head – Compliance, Legal & FCU immediately; fraud reported to UIDAI and the Aadhaar number holder with full details without undue delay. 3. Frequency of Aadhaar-related fraud reporting: immediate upon detection. 
4. CISO/Networking/Technology team responsible for escalation of misuse of information or systems related to Aadhaar framework within network. 
5. Cases at new business stage involving suspected Aadhaar misuse referred to FCU by Underwriting.
Empanelment of FCU investigators & its pay-out and recovery, penalty
Unreliable or Underperforming Investigation Agencies Leading to Incorrect Findings / Policy Decisions

Policy decisions (rejection, CFI, repudiation) are based entirely on investigation agency findings. Poor quality, delayed, or incorrect investigation reports (due to inadequate empanelment criteria, lack of SLAs, or absence of performance monitoring) lead to incorrect policy decisions, fraudulent claims being paid, and genuine claims being wrongly rejected.

1. Agencies empanelled per expertise, geographical reach, efficiency, accuracy, and quality (DVP to Sr. Manager responsible for empanelment of new agencies). 
2. Cases assigned to agencies via email with: referral no., in-date, customer name, address/contact, agency name, investigation type, gist, policy no. TAT defined in respective SLAs; TAT starts from day of referral. 
3. Specific investigation parameters mentioned at time of assignment. 
4. Agency acknowledges receipt; non-serviceable locations flagged same day. Investigation report drafted in Company-specified format, attested by authorised signatory. Findings stored in tracking worksheet with: gist, agency remarks, policy decision, closure TAT, TAT status, billing status. 
5. Positive cases randomly reinvestigated monthly with other agencies/customer calling for quality assurance; notable discrepancy triggers feedback to agency. Notarised affidavit required if findings not supported by strong documentary evidence. 
6. External investigation agency is maker; employee checker reviews report; supervisor reviews. 
7. Bills subject to 3-level verification (preparation, review, approve) before Accounts payment. Agency quarterly evaluation and monthly dashboard published. Performance assessment half-yearly.
Review of Follow-up and monitoring of frauds process
Fraudsters Not Prosecuted / Losses Not Recovered Due to Inadequate Legal Action

Failure to file timely FIRs/police complaints (threshold ₹50,000) or coordinate with law enforcement agencies may result in fraudsters evading consequences, non-recovery of misappropriated funds, and absence of deterrent effect. Failure to track loss recovery may lead to unmonitored outstanding fraud losses.

1. FCU initiates demand notice (sent through legal team) → legal notice → police complaint/FIR against accused in all financial misappropriation cases where amount ≥₹50,000 per internally approved procedure. 
2. Decision to prosecute or refer to law enforcement made in conjunction with legal counsel and senior management based on case disposition. 
3. FCU maintains tracker of all losses to be recovered from fraudsters and monitors periodically. 
4. Regular follow-ups with respective law enforcement agencies for timely deterrent action and recovery.
Review of Follow-up and monitoring of frauds process
Fraud Cases Not Recorded Systematically / TAT Breaches Not Identified

Failure to record all fraud cases in the Fraud Monitoring & Reporting System (FRMS) or daily tracker results in incomplete case database, missed follow-ups, TAT breaches, inability to identify fraud trends/patterns, and inadequate MIS for senior management and regulatory reporting.

1. All cases received at FCU recorded in FRMS by respective team members for case management (improves speed and efficiency in investigations and dashboards). 
2. Daily tracker maintained and records all cases from various channels. Database subjected to different parameters to observe trends, build reports, generate alerts, and establish patterns. 
3. Alerts shared with respective stakeholders for additional scrutiny. Daily alerts generated from FRMS to monitor case management and timely action. 
4. Trend analysis conducted monthly/quarterly/as-needed. Zonal dashboards prepared and published per timelines by DVP to Sr. Manager. 
5. FCU MIS (Monthly/Quarterly) presented to senior management; also published to business heads/regional teams with observations and recommendations.
Review of Follow-up and monitoring of frauds process
Non-Submission or Inaccurate IRDAI Fraud Monitoring Returns (FMR 1 / FMR 2)

Failure to file FMR 1 (outstanding fraud cases) and FMR 2 (closed fraud cases) with IRDAI within 30 days of financial year-end, or filing with incorrect categorisation (fraudulent death claims, medical non-disclosure, document/signature forgery, misrepresentation, premium misappropriation, PMJJBY cases), constitutes regulatory non-compliance under IRDAI Circular IRDA/SDD/MISC/CIR/009/01/2013, resulting in regulatory penalties and governance failures.

1. FCU compiles fraud statistics on all cases investigated/highlighted and action taken. Reported to IRDAI in FMR 1 (outstanding fraud cases) and FMR 2 (closed fraud cases) every year within 30 days of close of financial year per IRDAI Circular IRDA/SDD/MISC/CIR/009/01/2013.
2. Reporting categories: Death prior to proposal, Medical Non-Disclosure, Death Certificate fabricated, Previous insurance policies/suspicious cases, Group/PMJJBY claims (alive cases, fake death certificates), Medical Non-Disclosure; Signature Forgery, Document Forgery, Misrepresentation, Premium Misappropriation. Sub-categorisation by case source (claims-related; before-claims stage) and involvement (employee/intermediary/policyholder). 
3. Reports provided to Compliance team for regulatory submission.
Review of Follow-up and monitoring of frauds process
Internal Financial Controls Over Fraud Risk Not Assessed or Reported to Board/Auditors

Under Companies Act 2013, management and Board must implement Internal Financial Controls and ensure adequacy. If FCU does not prepare the IFCS annually and does not conduct fraud controls review (RAG scoring), auditors cannot express an opinion on effectiveness of IFC over financial reporting, resulting in governance gaps, audit qualifications, and regulatory non-compliance.

1. FCU prepares Internal Financial Control Sheet (IFCS) for the financial year in coordination with Internal Audit Department. 
2. Annual Fraud Controls Review: RAG scoring matrix to assess strength of fraud prevention and detection system (Red: substantial strengthening needed; Amber: some strengthening needed; Green: fraud risk reduced to minimally acceptable level). 
3.. Department reviews other initiatives per management directive in consultation with Risk team.

Non-availability of an established, approved, and updated policy framework and related processes may result in inconsistent operations, regulatory non-compliance, and increased risk of fraud or misstatement.

Approved policies and procedures are established, documented, and communicated to all relevant users to ensure consistent banking operations. The SOP covers all core banking activities including fund management, bank reconciliation, fund transfers, and balance confirmation.
Inadequate Organisation Structure with Ambiguous Roles and Responsibilities

An inadequate or informal organisation structure with unclear roles and responsibilities can cause confusion, duplication of effort, gaps in control coverage, and increased risk of unauthorized transactions.

A formal organisation structure is documented and approved with clearly defined roles and responsibilities for all levels (SVP, AVP, Deputy Manager, Team Members). Roles and responsibilities are communicated to all team members and reviewed periodically.
Outdated Policies and Procedures Without Periodic Review

Failure to update documented policies and procedures to reflect changing business conditions, regulatory requirements, or new banking products may lead to non-compliance, operational gaps, and audit observations.

The SOP is reviewed and updated at least annually (or when triggered by business or regulatory changes). Formal authorization is obtained from the CE Head. Superseded sections are replaced, new sections are inserted, and all changes are communicated to impacted stakeholders. Version history is maintained.
Inadequate Staff Training on Banking SOPs and Systems

Lack of structured training on banking SOPs, systems (Sun System, Vision, Net Banking), and authorization matrices may lead to processing errors, unauthorized transactions, and regulatory non-compliance.

Finance team members undergo structured onboarding training on the Banking SOP, systems (Sun System, Vision), and authorization matrices. Periodic refresher training is conducted when processes or systems change. Training records are maintained.
Delay or Failure in Extraction or Incorrect Transfer of Funds - Collection Accounts

Bank statements may not be extracted timely or entries may be incorrectly passed, leading to delays in fund transfer to the Investment team, misstatements in the Collection MIS, and financial reporting errors.

Finance team extracts bank statements of all collection accounts (excluding RRBs) in the first hour of each working day. For RRBs, funds are transferred by respective banks to HO payment accounts. Effective balance is checked for all accounts and a fund flow summary is prepared in Excel format and shared with the Investment team in the first hour of the next working day via email. Fund transfers are executed online or via letters/cheques for RTGS.
Insufficient Buffer Balance or Liquidity Mismatch in Collection Accounts

Failure to maintain the minimum buffer balance of Rs.50,000 in each collection account, or transferring entire RRB funds incorrectly, may cause overdrafts, liquidity gaps, or regulatory non-compliance.

Finance team maintains a minimum buffer of Rs.50,000 in each collection account daily. For RRB accounts, the entire fund is transferred to investment accounts without any buffer. The fund flow summary reflects effective balance after buffer deduction for non-RRB accounts. Internal approval note is prepared before executing transfers.
Unauthorized Transfers or Delayed Fund Flow Communication to Investment Team

Funds may be transferred without appropriate authorization as per the approval matrix, or the fund flow summary may not reach the Investment team timely, impacting investment operations and compliance.

Finance team prepares an internal approval note before executing fund transfers from collection accounts. Transfers are executed strictly per the authorization matrix: payments up to Rs.5 crore require any two Group A or Group B signatories; above Rs.5 crore require at least one Group A signatory. Fund flow summary is shared with Investment team via email in the first hour of the next working day. UTR is communicated to Investment team post-debit confirmation.
Delay or Incorrect Execution of Morning and Evening Fund Transfers to Investment

Fund transfers may be delayed, incorrectly executed, or not communicated, impacting investment operations and tri-party repo management. There are two transfers daily: morning (previous day collections) and evening (tri-party repo in multiples of Rs.5 lakh).

Finance team executes fund transfers online (or via letters/cheques for RTGS). Morning transfer covers previous day collections; evening tri-party repo transfer is in multiples of Rs.5 lakh with Investment team intimated at 2 PM. Debit confirmation is checked and UTR is communicated to Investment team via email. Journal entry is passed in Sun System and printout is filed for record.
Inaccurate or Incomplete Collection MIS Shared with Finance Team

Errors or omissions in the Collection MIS prepared and sent to the Finance team for passing necessary collection entries in Life Asia may result in incorrect or incomplete accounting entries and reconciliation mismatches.

Bank statement of all collection accounts (excluding RRBs) is extracted for the previous date. All debit and credit transactions are reviewed. Post review, MIS statement is prepared and verified for accuracy before being sent to the Finance team for passing necessary collection entries in Life Asia. RRB bank statements are updated based on receipt from respective nodal officers.
Misstatement Due to Unreconciled Bank and Book Balances
Failure to reconcile bank and book balances on a daily basis may lead to errors in financial reporting, undetected fraud, and accumulation of unresolved open items.

Finance team extracts bank statements (excluding RRBs) for the previous day and saves them to the server. Bank book is extracted from Sun System and book balance is arrived at for each collection account. Bank Reconciliation Statement is prepared in the standard Format II and circulated internally and to the Finance team. Banking team reconciles and prepares a listing of differences between bank credits and Life Asia entries for further action by Finance team.
Unidentified Debits or Credits Not Investigated and Followed Up Timely

Unidentified or unresolved transactions in bank accounts (e.g., unidentified credits, cheques issued but not presented, book-bank differences) may remain outstanding, leading to misstatements and audit findings.

Finance team knocks off book transactions against bank debits/credits or book reversals. Follow-up is done with banks for unidentified debits/credits. After identifying open items, necessary entries are passed in Sun System. Bank charges in collection accounts are accounted in Sun System (Dr: Bank Charges A/c; Cr: Respective Bank A/c) posted by checker. Reconciliation is published by EOD to the Accounts team. Two Excel sheets are maintained: internal working file and final reconciliation for circulation.
Stale Cheques Not Identified and Transferred to Stale Account Timely
Cheques outstanding for more than 3 months not being transferred to the stale account for refund/claim/vendor may result in misstated liabilities and unresolved open items in bank reconciliation.

Finance team monitors all issued cheques through the bank reconciliation process. Cheques outstanding for more than 3 months are identified during daily reconciliation and transferred to the stale account for refund/claim/vendor processing. This is tracked as a separate open item in the reconciliation and followed up with the concerned team.
Unauthorized or Incorrect Fund Transfers from Collection Accounts

Funds may be transferred from collection accounts without proper authorization, to incorrect accounts (non-SUD accounts), or outside approved signatory limits, leading to financial loss, regulatory non-compliance, and reputational damage.

Finance team executes fund transfers from collection accounts to Deutsche Bank account strictly per the authorization matrix. Payments up to Rs.5 crore: any two signatories from Group A or B; above Rs.5 crore: at least one Group A signatory. No direct third-party payments from collection accounts - only intra-SUD transfers are permitted. Inputter initiates and at least two approvers independently verify all details (account numbers, bank name, amount) before approving.
Direct Third-Party Payment Executed from Collection Account
Execution of a direct payment to a third party from a collection account (restricted to intra-SUD transfers only) could result in unauthorized outflow, fraud, and regulatory non-compliance.

Collection accounts are restricted to transfers only to another SUD bank account. This restriction is documented in the SOP and enforced through the authorization matrix. All transfers are reviewed by two approvers who verify the recipient account number and bank details before approval. Any deviation is escalated immediately to senior management.
Ineffective Cash Management or Unutilized Balances in Payment Accounts

Failure to prepare, review, or share the daily fund flow summary for payment/refund/claim accounts may lead to poor cash utilization, delayed payouts, and idle funds not being transferred to investment.

Finance team prepares the fund flow statement daily for all payment/refund/claim accounts (BOI, UBI, HDFC, Deutsche Bank). Statement is shared internally with senior authority, opex, and payout teams. Reasons for unutilized balances are inquired with concerned teams. MIS report is prepared capturing exceptional reasons for unspent balances. HOD reviews funds lying in bank accounts on a regular basis and initiates necessary action.
Misstatement Due to Unreconciled Balances or Open Items in Payment Accounts
Failure to reconcile bank and book balances for HO payment accounts on a daily basis may lead to errors in reporting, accumulation of open items, and undetected unauthorized transactions.

Bank statement is extracted through net banking daily for all HO payment accounts (BOI, UBI, HDFC, Deutsche Bank) and saved in the respective folder on the server. Bank book is extracted from Sun System daily. Reasons for differences between book and bank are analyzed and entries are passed accordingly. Follow-up for open items is done daily. Reconciliation is published by EOD to the Accounts team.
Unidentified Credits in Payment Accounts Not Investigated Timely

Unidentified credits received in payment accounts (e.g., premium amounts credited without sufficient reference details) that are not investigated with the bank may remain unresolved, leading to reconciliation mismatches and potential misapplication of funds.

Finance team identifies unidentified credits in payment accounts during daily reconciliation. For each unidentified credit, the bank is contacted for details such as application number, policy number, customer name, debit account number, and branch details. Entries are passed only after identification. Items not identifiable are tracked as open items and escalated per the defined escalation matrix.
Incorrect or Unauthorized Online Fund Transfers
Online fund transfers (inter-bank and intra-bank) may be executed incorrectly, without proper authorization, or to wrong account numbers, leading to financial loss or misdirected funds.

Finance team executes online fund transfers for inter-bank and intra-bank transactions using net banking facility. Transfers are executed strictly per the authorization matrix with inputter-approver segregation. Approvers verify all details (account number, bank name, IFSC, amount) before approving. Net banking facility is available only for collection and payment accounts.
Unauthorized Payments or Payments Outside Approved Limits - Payment Accounts

Payments may be executed without proper authorization or outside approved signatory limits for different payment categories (Refund/Claims, Payment A/c, Tax, Commission), leading to financial loss and non-compliance.

Finance team executes payments from HO payment accounts strictly as per four authorization matrices: (I) Refund & Claims: up to Rs.1 crore (any 2 of A/B), Rs.1-2 crore (min 1 Group A), above Rs.2 crore (MD/CEO or Dy.CEO/CFO); (II) Payment A/c: up to Rs.20L (any 2 A/B), Rs.20L-Rs.1 crore (min 1 Group A), above Rs.1 crore (MD/CEO or Dy.CEO/CFO); (III) Tax: up to Rs.20L (any 2 A/B), Rs.20L-Rs.5 crore (min 1 Group A), above Rs.5 crore (MD/CEO or Dy.CEO/CFO); (IV) Commission: up to Rs.50L (any 2 A/B), Rs.50L-Rs.5 crore (min 1 Group A), Rs.5-10 crore (both Group A), above Rs.10 crore (MD/CEO or Dy.CEO/CFO). Joint signature is mandatory for all categories.
Lack of Segregation of Duties Between Inputter and Approver for Fund Transfers
The same individual initiating (inputter) and approving (authorizer) a fund transfer defeats the maker-checker control and creates risk of unauthorized transfers or fraud.

For all fund transfers from collection and payment accounts, there is a designated inputter who initiates the transaction and at least two separate approvers who review and approve. The inputter cannot be one of the approvers. System access controls on net banking platforms enforce this segregation. Any deviation is escalated immediately to senior management.
Inaccurate or Missing Quarterly Balance Confirmations from Banks

Failure to obtain balance confirmation/certification from banks on a quarterly basis may lead to audit findings, inability to match closing balances, and misstatement of bank balances in financial statements.

Finance team obtains balance confirmation/certification from banks quarterly. Hard copies are received from the concerned bank branch for HO accounts. For RRBs, the Nodal Officer collects balance confirmations from respective RRBs and provides scan copies via mail or courier. Balance confirmations are attached with the Bank Reconciliation Statement and submitted to Auditors on a quarterly basis.
Mismatch Between Bank Balance Confirmation and Book Balance Not Investigated
A balance confirmation received from the bank that does not match the book balance in Sun System, if not investigated and resolved, may indicate unrecorded transactions, errors, or fraud.

Upon receipt of balance confirmation from banks, Finance team compares the certified bank balance with the book balance in Sun System as of the same date. Any differences are investigated and root cause identified (e.g., timing differences, unposted entries, errors). Reconciliation of balance confirmations with the Bank Reconciliation Statement is completed before submission to Auditors. Unresolved differences are escalated to the AVP.
Delay or Improper Documentation for New Bank Account Opening
Failure to file required documents correctly or timely may delay bank account opening or lead to non-compliance with banking and regulatory requirements.

Finance team prepares and files required documents with banks for opening new accounts. Office note is prepared and necessary approvals obtained before account opening. Finance team retains copies of all filed documents for record purposes.
Unauthorized or Unapproved Changes in Authorized Signatories
Changes to authorized signatories may be made without proper approval, enabling unauthorized access to bank accounts and potential fraudulent transfers.

Finance team prepares an office note for approval from MD & CEO for any changes to authorized signatories (as per Board Resolution passed at the 30th Board Meeting, 9 August 2011). A formal letter with photocopy of approved office note is sent to the bank. Bank authenticates changes by applying its seal acknowledging receipt. Changes in signatory limits per Board Resolutions are also communicated via separate letters.
Incorrect or Unauthorized Signatory Limits Communicated to Banks
Failure to update banks with revised signatory limits may lead to transactions being executed outside approved limits or non-compliance with Board Resolutions.

Finance team prepares and sends letters to banks communicating changes in signatory limits as per Board Resolutions. Letters are accompanied by relevant Board Resolution extracts and sent after obtaining required approvals. Acknowledgment from banks is retained on record.
IMPS transactions may be executed incorrectly, without proper authorization, or based on unverified data received from respective teams, leading to financial loss or misdirected funds.

Finance team executes IMPS transactions based on data received from respective teams. Finance team verifies all transaction details (account number, amount, beneficiary name, IFSC code) before execution. Authorization is obtained as per the applicable payment authorization matrix before processing. Executed transactions are confirmed and records are maintained.
Inaccurate or Incomplete Monthly Cash Flow Statement
Errors or omissions in the monthly cash flow statement related to banking transactions may result in misstated financials and incorrect management reporting.

Finance team prepares the monthly cash flow statement covering all banking transactions. The statement is reviewed by the Deputy Manager / AVP before submission. Supporting data is reconciled with Sun System entries and bank statements to ensure completeness and accuracy.
Inaccurate or Incomplete Related Party Disclosures and Notes to Accounts

Failure to accurately identify and disclose related party transactions and notes to accounts related to banking operations quarterly may result in non-compliance with Companies Act 2013 and financial misstatement.

Finance team identifies and compiles all related party transactions and other required notes to accounts related to banking operations on a quarterly basis. These are reviewed for accuracy and completeness by the Deputy Manager and AVP before submission for quarterly financial closing.
Failure to Complete Banking Reconciliation Within Defined TAT
Failure to publish bank reconciliation within T+1 (normal) or T+2 (abnormal) may result in delayed identification of discrepancies, accumulation of open items, and delayed financial closing.

Finance team tracks completion of banking reconciliation against defined TAT (T+1 normal, T+2 abnormal). In exceptional cases where reconciliation is not published, the reason is documented and updated to seniors. Delays are escalated per the matrix: Level 1 (Deputy Manager), Level 2 (AVP), Level 3 (SVP Finance & Accounts). Overall TAT achievement of 95% is measured quarterly.
Failure to Execute Collection Fund Transfer Within Defined TAT
Failure to transfer collection funds to the Investment team within T (normal) or T+1 (abnormal) may result in missed investment opportunities, idle cash, and investment return leakage.

Finance team monitors execution of both morning and evening collection fund transfers against defined TAT. Any delay is documented with reason and escalated per the escalation matrix. Investment team intimation for evening tri-party repo is done at 2 PM based on actual collection.
Unauthorized Net Banking Access or Cyber Fraud Risk
Unauthorized access to net banking accounts used for fund transfers, or phishing/cyber attacks on banking credentials, may result in fraudulent transactions, financial loss, and reputational damage.

Net banking facility is available only for collection and payment accounts and access is restricted to authorized Finance team members. Multi-factor authentication and inputter-approver segregation are enforced on net banking platforms. Net banking credentials are not shared and are changed periodically. Suspicious transactions or access alerts from the bank are investigated immediately and reported to senior management.
Inadequate Record Maintenance of Banking Documents

Failure to maintain banking records (bank statements, reconciliations, balance confirmations, fund flow summaries, authorization notes) systematically and securely for the required 8-year retention period under Section 128 of the Companies Act 2013 may result in audit findings and regulatory non-compliance.

Finance team ensures all banking-related data and files (bank statements, reconciliations, balance confirmations, audit data files, regulatory reports) are preserved in dedicated folders on the shared drive ('Accounts Folder') in a systematic manner. Files are classified as Internal and stored in soft copy on the Share Drive. Records are retained for 8 years as required under Section 128 of the Companies Act 2013.
Insider Fraud or Collusion in Fund Transfers and Banking Operations

An authorized team member with access to net banking, Sun System entries, and fund transfer instructions may independently or collusively initiate fraudulent transfers, manipulate book entries, or misappropriate funds.

(i) Mandatory inputter-approver segregation with at least two approvers for all fund transfers. (ii) Joint signatory requirement enforced per payment category with amount-specific escalation to senior signatories. (iii) No direct third-party payments from collection accounts. (iv) Daily fund flow summary reviewed by HOD providing management oversight. (v) Daily bank reconciliation published to Accounts team for independent review. (vi) Approvers independently verify all transfer details before approving. (vii) UTR confirmation communicated to Investment team as independent transaction evidence.
Non-compliance with IRDAI Regulations on Payment of Commission & Appointment of Agents

Failure to establish, approve, or implement a board-approved policy for payment of commission and appointment of agents/intermediaries as per IRDAI (Payment of Commission) Regulations 2023 may lead to regulatory non-compliance, penalties, reputational damage, and operational inefficiencies.

Board approves the written policy for payment of commission and appointment of agents/intermediaries as mandated by IRDAI (Payment of Commission) Regulations 2023 (effective 1 Apr 2023). Policy covers eligibility, remuneration structure, termination/suspension/cancellation of appointment, MBG norms, and EOM caps. Policy is reviewed at least every three years; version control and change log maintained. Compliance team monitors adherence to IRDAI regulations.
Inaccurate or Incomplete Commission Expense Recording

Commission expenses may be misstated if amounts recorded in Sun (GL) do not agree with CMS (source commission transactions), leading to financial reporting errors, regulatory non-compliance, and potential mispayments or under/over-accruals.

Distribution team extracts policy-level commission transaction data from CMS and aggregates it to total commission for the period. This is reconciled against commission expense booked in Sun for the same period. Any variance beyond defined thresholds is investigated and communicated to IT/Operations for correction in CMS/Sun, with adjustments posted and evidence retained. Reconciliation is performed monthly.

Commission payouts may be misstated or unauthorised if recoveries/holds/releases and TDS are not applied correctly, or if payment advice is not properly reviewed and approved by designated authorities, leading to over/under payments, tax non-compliance, financial misstatement, partner disputes, and regulatory issues.

Distribution team computes gross commission and applicable TDS, adjusts for recovery items, current holds, earlier holds and releases to arrive at net payable. A partner-wise payment advice is prepared, reviewed, and approved by designated authorities per DOA. Approved advice and supporting schedules are sent to F&A for payment execution. F&A validates advice before posting entries.
Non-compliance with Professional Tax Regulations – Karnataka

Failure to correctly deduct and remit Professional Tax for agents in Karnataka may result in statutory non-compliance, regulatory penalties or interest charges. Karnataka PT rules: deduct ₹1,500 annually when YTD commission exceeds ₹36,000; agents above 65 years are exempt.

Distribution team monitors agent commission earnings and applies PT deductions as per Karnataka and Maharashta state rules. PT of ₹1,500 and ₹2,500 respectively is deducted annually when YTD commission exceeds ₹36,000; agents above 65 are exempt. PT deducted from commission payouts and remitted to state authorities. Documentation of calculations, deductions, and payments is maintained.
Misstatement of Commission Expenses due to Incorrect Booking or Non-Reversal

Commission expenses may be misstated if automated uploads (LA & GA) are incomplete/incorrect, manual GSLI calculations are inaccurate or unapproved, or reversals for terminated agents are not recorded in the same period — resulting in over/understatement of expenses, regulatory non-compliance, and potential partner disputes.

Automated (LA & GA): Commission generated automatically based on premium issuance/cancellation; Policy Accounting team uploads daily system files to book commission in GL using prescribed GL codes (4010100010/20/30 series; 2050100XXX). Manual (GSLI): Distribution team calculates manually; F&A books at payout on approved documentation. Reversals: Terminated agent commissions reversed in same period. All uploads, manual calculations, approvals, and reversals documented and retained.
Incorrect or Unapproved Commission Disbursement Entries

If F&A posts transfer entries without proper validation against the approved payment advice and reconciled commission liability, or misapplies TDS/PT, commissions may be misstated, statutory liabilities incorrect, and payments over/under — leading to financial reporting errors, tax non-compliance, and partner disputes.

F&A verifies amounts against reconciled commission liability in LA/GA and the approved advice (including TDS and PT schedules). Posts accounting entries to transfer commission from Commission Payable GL to partner settlement/payable accounts, net of statutory deductions. Records TDS liability in GL 2050502010 and PT in respective statutory GLs. Performs control check ensuring gross, deductions and net totals match advice; obtains reviewer approval before finalisation. Evidence retained.
Incorrect or Unauthorised Commission Disbursements via Bank Transfers / NEFT

Payments may be misstated, misdirected, or unauthorised if funds are called without proper validation, consolidated/branch-wise instructions are inaccurate, or bank execution deviates from approved payment advice, leading to over/under payments, operational losses, partner disputes, and control account reconciliation issues.

F&A calls for required funds in designated bank accounts prior to payment execution. Payments executed through BOI (consolidated transfer letter; branch-wise instructions shared by Distribution directly to bank), UBI (consolidated letter with Digital Authority Signature; branch-wise instructions), BOI/UBI-controlled RRBs (transfer letters crediting respective RRB accounts), and bulk NEFT/Transfer for CA/Broker/Tied Agency channels. All transfer letters authorised per DOA; execution confirmed by bank and reconciled.
Non-Submission or Delayed IRDAI Commission Payment Returns

Failure to prepare, review, approve, or file the annual commission payment returns per IRDAI timeline (within 45 days of FY-end) and governance requirements may result in regulatory penalties, reduced oversight, and weakened corporate governance.

Finance prepares annual IRDAI commission payment returns (Schedule V) in Board-approved format based on verified payout data. Returns submitted to Audit Committee for review; observations tracked and closed. Post Audit Committee review, returns placed before Board for approval. Upon Board approval, returns filed with IRDAI within 45 days from FY-end. Distribution team validates Form 6A. Supporting records (workings, AC minutes, Board resolutions, IRDAI submission acknowledgements) retained.

Non-adherence to defined TATs for commission payout activities may result in delayed payments to agents/intermediaries, leading to partner dissatisfaction, reputational damage, operational inefficiencies, and potential regulatory non-compliance.

Company-defined TATs: T+2 – IT provides commission data; T+3 – Distribution reconciles with Sun; T+4 – Distribution calculates holds, releases, TDS, PT; T+5 – Distribution prepares approval note and informs F&A; T+6 – F&A validates payment advice; T+7 – F&A executes final payout and posts accounting entries. (T = system closure date.) Delays escalated per escalation matrix: Level 1 – Dy. Manager/Manager; Level 2 – Sr. Manager/AVP; Level 3 – VP/SVP.
Lack of Timely Payment Confirmation / Incomplete Records

Failure to provide timely and accurate payment confirmation with bank references may lead to incomplete payout records, delayed reconciliation, partner disputes, operational inefficiencies, and delays in resolving partner queries.

After executing commission payments, F&A team confirms completion to Distribution team and shares bank reference numbers (UTR/transaction IDs) for each payment. Record of confirmation emails and reference details maintained for reconciliation and audit purposes.

If commission payable GLs are not reconciled accurately and timely, discrepancies may remain unresolved, leading to misstated liabilities, incorrect payouts, financial reporting errors, and potential regulatory non-compliance.

On a quarterly basis: (a) Extract all commission expense GLs from Sun; (b) Extract all commission liability GLs from Sun; (c) Obtain hold commission summary and listing from Distribution; (d) Reconcile hold/release details with Sun balances and identify gaps; (e) Post rectification/reclassification entries in Sun. Separate reconciliations prepared for individual and group commission payable GLs. Evidence of reconciliation, adjustments, and approvals retained.
Commission Written Off / Written Back & Provisions
Incorrect or Delayed Provisioning & Write-Off of Commission Recoveries
Failure to apply aging rules accurately or obtain proper approvals for provisioning/write-offs may result in misstated financials, regulatory non-compliance, and operational inefficiencies.

Debit balances from cancelled policies carried forward and recovered from subsequent commissions. Aging rules: Active agents/brokers/CA – no action up to 6 months; provision 6–12 months; write-off beyond 12 months. Terminated/expired agents – immediate write-off. GL entries: Bad debts (4021700010 Dr / 2050100XXX Cr) for write-off; Provision (4060000035 Dr / 2060300035 Cr) for provision. Distribution monitors aging and prepares schedules; F&A posts after designated authority approval. Evidence includes aging reports, approval notes, and JVs.
Commission Written Off / Written Back & Provisions
Incorrect or Delayed Write-Back of Held Commission
Failure to accurately identify and write back held commission amounts within defined timelines may result in misstated liabilities, regulatory non-compliance, and operational inefficiencies.

Commission held and written back from date of transaction under conditions: (a) License expiry – all outstanding commission written back; (b) Own Policy Rule – held until 6 other policies sourced within 1 agency year, else written back at year-end; (c) MBG shortfall – held until MBG met, written back after 2 unsuccessful MBG years; (d) Non-receipt of old IRDA licence – written back after 3 years; (e) Bank rejection – written back after 3 years. GL entries: 2050100XXX Dr / 3030300025 Cr (write-back); 2050100026 Dr / 3020600011 Cr (bank rejection). Distribution monitors conditions, prepares schedules; F&A posts approved write-back entries. Evidence retained.
Commission Written Off / Written Back & Provisions
Incorrect or Unauthorised Commission Write-Off / Write-Back Accounting

If write-offs and write-backs are processed without proper quarterly reconciliation, approval, or consistent accounting treatment, liabilities and expenses may be misstated; subsequent recoveries/payments may be recorded in the wrong period, leading to financial reporting errors, control breakdowns, and audit issues.

Distribution and F&A perform quarterly commission payable reconciliation identifying items for recovery, write-off, or write-back. Joint approval note prepared post reconciliation; signed off by designated authority. F&A posts write-off/write-back entries in GL on quarterly basis; Distribution carries forward operational balances for future recovery/payment tracking. Amounts subsequently recovered or paid recognised in the quarter they occur. Documentation: reconciliation schedules, approval notes, JVs, evidence of subsequent recoveries/payments retained.
Incorrect GST Calculation / Payment or Non-Compliance

Failure to correctly calculate, account, or pay GST on commission payouts (different mechanisms for Banca, Agency, Brokers/CA) may lead to tax non-compliance, penalties, interest, ITC loss, and financial reporting errors.

Banca: GST @18% calculated on actual commission paid based on customer state; paid to banks; banks issue GST invoices to Tax team. Agency: GST computed and accounted under RCM based on customer state; GL entries (4999999999 Dr contra; SGST/CGST/IGST Input Credit GLs Dr; CGST/SGST/IGST Payable – Commission Tied Agency Cr); paid directly to Government. Brokers/CA: GST reimbursed based on partner invoices. Distribution computes GST; shares with F&A for payment. Tax team ensures compliance and records invoices. Evidence: GST calculation sheets, invoices, payment challans, reconciliations.
Incorrect Commission Rates Applied – Over/Under Payment

Incorrect commission criteria or rates may be applied (e.g., wrong product, wrong channel, wrong year of policy) due to errors in commission table setup in LA/GA or manual override, resulting in inaccurate payouts to agents, financial misstatement, and potential regulatory non-compliance with EOM caps.

Distribution team reviews commission rates applied to payouts on a sample basis every cycle, cross-checking against the approved commission table set up in the system. Any rate variance identified is escalated to IT for correction and a revised payment advice is issued. Maker-checker control within Distribution: Maker computes; Checker (F&A) validates before approval. All rate changes in the system must be authorised per DOA and subject to UAT before deployment.
Arithmetic / Formula Errors in Commission Calculation

Calculation or formula errors in the Distribution team's payment working (holds, releases, TDS, PT) may lead to incorrect commission amounts being paid, resulting in partner disputes, financial misstatement, and over/under-deduction of statutory amounts.

Distribution team (Maker) computes gross commission, holds, releases, TDS, and PT using standardised working templates. F&A team (Checker) independently validates computations against source data (CMS extract, approved commission table, TDS rate schedule, PT eligibility list) before issuing the payment advice. Any discrepancy between Maker and Checker outputs is escalated for correction before payment. Approved payment working retained as audit evidence.
Commission Credited to Wrong / Closed Bank Account

Commission may be credited to an incorrect or closed bank account due to stale bank details in CMS, failure to update after account changes, or data entry errors in the payment instruction, leading to financial loss, partner disputes, and reconciliation failures.

CMS maintains agent bank account details; updates to bank accounts require approved documentation and are subject to dual control before update in the system. Distribution team prepares partner-wise payment advice using CMS-verified bank details. Bank rejections (failed NEFT/transfers) are identified by F&A post-execution; rejection amounts carried forward and written back after 3 years if unclaimed. Bank rejection listing maintained and reviewed quarterly. Bulk NEFT file validated before submission.
Commission Written Off / Written Back & Provisions
Commission Clawback Not Performed or Incorrectly Computed

When policies are cancelled post commission payout, commission (along with TDS and PT) must be recovered from subsequent payouts. Failure to identify cancellations, incorrect calculation of recovery amounts, or omission of TDS/PT recovery components results in unrecovered commission, overstated expenses, and financial loss.

Quarterly review of all outstanding commission payables to Agents/Brokers/CA to identify amounts requiring clawback following policy cancellations. Distribution team maintains a recovery (debit balance) schedule and carries forward uncovered amounts for recovery from subsequent commissions. TDS and PT recovered proportionately. Aging applied: no action up to 6 months; provision 6–12 months; write-off beyond 12 months. Clawback calculations approved by designated authority; journal vouchers and aging reports retained.
Incorrect GST State Mapping or Mechanism (RCM vs Forward Charge)

Incorrect GST classification (RCM for agency vs forward charge for Banca/Brokers/CA) or wrong state mapping for place of supply determination may result in incorrect CGST/SGST/IGST split, incorrect ITC claims, non-compliance, penalties, and interest.

Monthly review ensures GST is computed and accounted correctly based on partner type (Banca → forward charge @18%; Agency → RCM; Brokers/CA → based on partner invoice) and customer state for place of supply. Distribution team provides state-wise commission breakdowns; Taxation team verifies GST mechanism and state allocation before payment. Any mismatch between GL entries and GSTR workings escalated for correction. GST reconciliation performed monthly with GSTR 3B.
Delayed or Inaccurate MIS / Regulatory Reports

Failure to prepare and submit accurate MIS reports (commission policy-level data, bad debts schedule, provision schedule, bank rejection listing) and regulatory returns (IRDAI Schedule V by 31 May) on time may result in audit exceptions, regulatory penalties, and governance failures.

Commission EOD report prepared daily. Quarterly MIS: commission policy-level data (individual & group), bad debts written-off schedule, provision written-back schedule, agent provision schedule, agent balance schedules 12 & 13, bank rejection listing, related party schedule. IRDAI Schedule V filed on or before 31 May each year; Distribution team validates Form 6A. All reports reviewed and approved before submission. Submission acknowledgements and supporting workings retained.
Unresolved Discrepancies / Delays due to Absence of Escalation

Delays or errors in commission processing, reconciliation, or payment may remain unresolved if no clear escalation path exists, resulting in partner dissatisfaction, regulatory breaches, and financial misstatement.

Defined escalation matrix for commission processing, reconciliation, and payment issues: Level 1 – Deputy Manager/Manager; Level 2 – Senior Manager/AVP; Level 3 – Vice President/SVP. Issues unresolved within TAT escalated to next level. Escalation logs maintained and reviewed. EOD confirmation report prepared daily and shared with appropriate authority.
Non-availability of established and updated policy framework
Risk of non-availability of established and updated policy framework and related processes; risk assessment not carried out at the time of process modification.

Approved policies and procedures are established, documented, and communicated to all relevant users to ensure consistent and compliant operations. These policies define the standard operating framework for the process and are reviewed periodically to remain current with regulatory and business requirements.
Inadequate / informal organisation structure; ambiguity in roles & responsibilities

An inadequate or informal organisation structure with unclear roles and responsibilities can cause confusion, duplication of work, delays, and missed controls, leading to operational inefficiencies and compliance gaps.

A formal organisation structure is documented and approved, with clearly defined roles and responsibilities for all positions. Organisation charts are maintained and communicated to relevant stakeholders. Any changes follow a formal approval process.
Outdated policies and procedures; absence of periodic review
Failure to update documented policies & procedures to reflect changing business conditions and regulations in the absence of periodic review.
The policies and procedures are updated as and when required with changing business needs and regulations. The SOP is reviewed and approved annually.
Financial statement misstatement due to expense misclassification
If expenses are not classified correctly as Capex or Opex, assets, depreciation, or operating costs may be recorded wrongly, rendering financial statements inaccurate.

The Finance team checks every expense and classifies it as either Capex or Opex. Capex items (furniture, laptops, cars, software) are added to the asset register and depreciated monthly as per policy. Opex items (salaries, rent, travel, repairs) are booked as expenses in the same period incurred.
Compliance and documentation risk in expense classification
If expense classifications are not properly validated or reviewed, records may be inaccurate, policies may be breached, and compliance or documentation issues may arise.
The Finance team validates the classification with appropriate supporting documents, and periodic reviews are conducted to ensure accuracy, compliance, and proper record-keeping.
Unauthorised approvals may lead to rule violations, inaccurate reporting, and breakdown of the approval process.
All expenses are approved as per Delegation of Authority (DOA) limits defined in VSM/EMS, with higher-value expenses escalated to the appropriate authority in line with hierarchy.
Unauthorised utility and vendor payment approval
Unauthorised or invalid approvals of utility bills and one-time vendor payments may lead to non-compliance, financial errors, or lack of proper documentation.
Finance team ensures approvals for utility bills and one-time vendor payments are obtained through valid DOA mail or hard copy.
Incorrect or unauthorised employee expense bookings may lead to policy non-compliance, financial misstatements, or unapproved reimbursements.
The Finance team checks employee entitlements when booking expenses, based on the reimbursement policy set by HR. Any deviation requires HOD/HR approval before processing.
Lack of document validation in payouts
Payments or reimbursements may be processed without proper supporting documents, leading to invalid, duplicate, or fraudulent claims.
Finance validates supporting documents in EMS/VSM before approving any payout or reimbursement.
Incorrect GL / T-code selection causing misclassification in books
Use of wrong GL codes or T-codes can result in incorrect expense classification across departments, channels, and business lines, leading to misstated financials and unreliable MIS.

Finance team selects proper GL codes and T-codes for each transaction based on nature of expense and SUN system mapping. A second person (Checker) reviews all entries before posting. SUN system prevents the same user from inputting and posting.
Non-compliance in TDS and GST leading to penalties
Incorrect TDS rates, missing reverse-charge entries, or wrong GST state codes can attract statutory notices, interest, and penalties.

Finance checks TDS applicability and rate for each vendor payment. GST numbers, addresses, and applicable codes (CGST/SGST/IGST/RCM) are validated before posting. System-defined TDS and GST rules (updated by Taxation team) auto-populate in VSM. Lower-deduction certificates are tracked against limits.
Unauthorised bank instructions or unupdated payment status
Bank instructions signed outside authorised limits or UTR numbers not updated in the register can result in control failures, stale payment statuses, and inability to trace payouts.

All bank payment files/letters are signed by authorised signatories as per the bank approval matrix (MD/CEO – no limit; VP & above – up to ₹1 Cr; below VP – up to ₹20 Lakh). UTR numbers from bank reverse-feed are updated manually in the inward register and shared with SPOCs.
Delays or lack of communication in payout timelines may result in late vendor/employee payments, strained relationships, or operational inefficiencies.
Finance ensures vendor payouts (T+4) and employee payouts (T+5) are processed within defined timelines, with weekly/month-end cycles communicated to SPOCs.
Absence of a defined escalation mechanism may result in delayed payouts going unresolved, impacting vendor/employee relations and audit trail.
Escalation emails are triggered post TAT breach: Level 1 – Manager; Level 2 – AVP; Level 3 – SVP, Finance & Accounts. Daily EOD report captures payout status and outstanding items.
Advances to employees/vendors and its settlement

Employee advances may not be settled within the defined timeline or recovered appropriately, leading to financial exposure, non-compliance with regulatory norms, and potential disputes during resignation.
Finance monitors and enforces settlement of employee advances within 15 days, following up on outstanding amounts and escalating unresolved cases to the respective HOD.
Advances to employees/vendors and its settlement
Advance not recovered upon employee exit
If outstanding advances are not identified and recovered at the time of F&F settlement, the organisation faces financial loss.
Finance team checks for outstanding advances in the respective Employee GL, Unpaid Salary Payable, and Staff Advance GL before processing F&F. Recovery is coordinated with HR.
Advances to employees/vendors and its settlement
Incorrect expense booking due to unsettled vendor advances
Vendor advances may not be properly supported, settled, or adjusted against tax invoices, leading to financial exposure, incorrect expense booking, and non-compliance with tax/GST requirements.
Refunds or payouts are adjusted only upon submission of the tax invoice, and expenses/GST input credit are booked strictly after receipt of the final tax invoice and settlement of the advance.
Advances to employees/vendors and its settlement
Incorrect period recognition of prepaid expenses
Prepaid amounts may be expensed upfront instead of being amortised, or the cut-off date may be applied incorrectly, leading to misstatement of expenses across periods.

Any payment above ₹50,000 for service extending beyond one month is booked as prepaid and amortised over the service period. Cut-off is the 15th of the month – service starting on or before the 15th is included in that month; after the 15th it starts from the next month.
DOA may not be properly documented or communicated, leading to officers approving expenses beyond their authorised limits.
Finance department maintains a centralised DOA register and communicates the approved limits to all relevant departments.
Financial transactions may be executed without adherence to approved DOA limits, resulting in regulatory non-compliance and governance lapses.
All financial transactions are validated against the DOA register prior to processing to ensure adherence to authorised limits.
Petty cash withdrawals or payments may exceed prescribed limits without proper approval, leading to unauthorised cash usage.
Petty cash withdrawal and payment limits are predefined (₹25,000 per withdrawal; ₹10,000 per transaction) and strictly enforced by Finance.
Inadequate recording and reconciliation of petty cash
Petty cash transactions may not be properly recorded in registers or reconciled, resulting in misstatement of accounts and audit issues.
Finance team maintains a dedicated petty cash register (Excel) to record all petty cash transactions on a real-time basis.
Lack of proper approval and oversight for petty cash
Petty cash expenses may be processed without required DOA or Finance Head approval, causing governance lapses and regulatory non-compliance.
Monthly petty cash expense statements are prepared and approved by the Finance Controller/Head, providing oversight and governance.
Foreign exchange may be issued to employees without adherence to HR Travel policy or DOA, leading to governance lapses and regulatory non-compliance.
Foreign exchange issuance to employees is strictly governed by the HR Travel Policy and Delegation of Authority.
Delayed or incomplete settlement of forex advances
Employees may fail to settle foreign exchange advances promptly after travel, causing misstatement of accounts, cash exposure, or misuse of funds.
Finance verifies settlement by reconciling advance issued versus actual expenses incurred, supported by bills/invoices.
Forex payouts to vendors may be made without adequate supporting documents or regulatory compliance, resulting in legal penalties.

Payments are routed through empaneled banks/remitters, ensuring exchange rates and documentation (Form 15CA, 15CB, 10F, TRC, Form A2, invoice, No PE declaration) are aligned with regulatory standards.
Incorrect exchange rate application in books
Transactions may be recorded at incorrect exchange rates (not as per bank advice), leading to inaccurate expense booking and financial misstatement.
Finance team verifies the exchange rate applied in the accounting system against the bank advice before posting entries.
Inadequate record-keeping for forex receipts and settlements
Forex receipts and settlements may not be properly documented or reconciled with empaneled vendors, causing traceability gaps and audit exceptions.
All foreign exchange receipts and settlements are documented with supporting bank advice, vendor invoices, and acknowledgment receipts.
Inaccurate processing or non-compliance in rental payments
Office rental payments may be inaccurately processed or non-compliant with TDS/GST, leading to financial misstatement or regulatory penalties.
GST payments are released to landlords strictly upon receipt of valid tax invoices, ensuring compliance.
Errors in rent computation and TDS deduction on rent
Incorrect rent calculations (including missed escalations) or wrong TDS deductions on rent payments can lead to financial misstatement and statutory non-compliance.

Finance verifies rent calculations received from Facility including start/end dates, escalations, and agreed amounts. TDS on rent is deducted as per applicable rates under Section 194-I. Entries are posted in SUN only after verification.
Payroll entry errors and approval gaps
Payroll entries from the outsourced vendor may be incorrect, unapproved, or wrongly uploaded, causing salary errors, funding issues, and reconciliation gaps.
Outsourced payroll vendor provides monthly accounting entries in uploadable format to Finance. Entries are approved by HR before upload into SUN. Finance and HR reconcile on a monthly basis.
Errors in Full & Final settlements and leave encashment
F&F settlements may be miscalculated, bulk uploads may have errors, or leave encashment may not be properly reconciled, leading to wrong employee payouts.

HR department prepares detailed F&F calculation sheets and ensures accuracy through review and approval before submission to Finance. Finance validates against Employee GL, Unpaid Salary Payable GL, and Staff Advance GL.
Errors in actuarial valuation and liability reporting
Actuarial valuations for leave encashment, gratuity, or long-term incentives may be missed or applied incorrectly, leading to wrong liability reporting and non-compliance with AS-15.

Actuarial valuation certificates for leave encashment, gratuity, and long-term incentives are obtained from the appointed actuary on a quarterly basis. Incremental liabilities are transferred to Trust accounts or carried forward as applicable.
Statutory payments (PF, ESIC, TDS, GST, PT, LWF) may be delayed, underpaid, or unsupported by proper challans, leading to regulatory non-compliance, penalties, and weakened documentation.

HR department prepares statutory payment details based on payroll and F&F records. Finance reconciles liabilities in SUN against HR workings and makes payments by due dates (PF/ESIC – 15th; TDS – 7th of following month). HR maintains challans.
Inaccurate provisioning for perks, F&F, and variable payouts
Provisions for perks, F&F, and variable payouts may be misstated or booked incorrectly, causing year-end financial errors and compliance gaps.

Finance team reviews provision schedules against payroll registers, employee contracts, and approval notes to ensure accuracy. Provisions are reversed in the following month (up to February) and booked on actual basis in March.
Fixed Asset Addition, Deletion and Depreciation
Incorrect asset classification (Capex vs. Opex; asset category)
Assets may be wrongly classified between Capex and Opex, or between categories (IT, Furniture, Leasehold, etc.), leading to misstatement of financials.

Finance team reviews all expense claims to determine whether they qualify as Capex or Opex based on accounting policy. Items below ₹1,000 individually are not capitalised. Correct asset category (Computer Hardware, Software, Furniture, AC, Leasehold, etc.) is assigned.
